catalog_quote: The distinctive prosodic features are intonation (at least the two types described in 2.1-2.2), tonality, and nasality. Two contrasting pitch-levels are distinguished (see sections 2.1, 2.45): a high or "normal" tone, unmarked, and a low tone, marked //. Tonality is an inherent feature of syllables in one or the other of its two values; nasality (marked /V̨/) is either present or absent. [p. 11] ... An examination of the prosodic features of Dogrib reveals an intonational structure which is superimposed upon a two-value tonal system, and which marks the intonational phrase (IP). [p. 4] ... Every IP, whether final or non-final, comprises one or more syllabic peaks, and exactly as many tones as syllabic peaks. [p. 8]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Dogrib (dogr1252) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Jaker 2012 'Prosodic reversal in Dogrib (Weledeh dialect)' (Stanford PhD, xiii+808 pp.org/Internet Archive copy); ProQuest 3497146 / OCLC 800721216 only. this search of works with stress in the title surfaced two further first-hand Weledeh stress sources by the same author: (a) Jaker 2017, 'Wıìlıìdeh Yahtıì Stress Revisited: Evidence for Iambic Foot Structure', Working Papers in Dene Languages 13 pp. 89-103 (ANLA CA001WP2017, print only — no digital file at ANLA), and (b) Jaker 2026, Linguistic Inquiry doi:10.1162/ling.a.556 (CC-BY), whose abstract (read via Crossref/Semantic Scholar; MIT Press could not be reached by automated download) states that Wıìlıìdeh has iambic stress which attracts Low tone early in the derivation while High tone attracts stress later — the mirror image of Tetsǫ́t’ıné. Papers read in full (Jaker & Howson 2022, Jaker 2023 AMP) concern Tetsǫ́t’ıné and never mention Dogrib; Jaker 2022 NLLT was reachable only as abstract + references (confirms the 2012 citation, surfaces Marinakis 2004 UVic MA thesis). Howren 1969 (Rae Dogrib, held by the project, read) lists intonation, tone and nasality as the distinctive prosodic features and is silent on stress. Best statement in hand: the Jaker 2026 abstract (iambic; tone-stress interaction), edge/position unspecified. Acquisition priority: high for Jaker 2012 (library/ProQuest), Jaker 2017 (ANLC print volume) and the Jaker 2026 PDF (open CC-BY, needs a non-blocked network); medium for Marinakis 2004. New files and records and logged in there.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Howren's first systematic phonology of (Rae) Dogrib treats the language as a two-tone language (high unmarked, low marked) with phrase-level intonation contours; stress is not among the distinctive prosodic features and is not mentioned at all, so no word-stress position can be read from any accessible source. The only explicit stress claim for the language is second-hand, from the CrossRef abstract of Jaker 2026 (Linguistic Inquiry): the Wıìlıìdeh (Weledeh, Yellowknives) dialect has iambic stress that interacts with (and early in the derivation attracts) Low tone, and Jaker 2012 (808-page Stanford dissertation) is the full account; neither could be opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. Howren notes tonal allophony conditioned by intonational-phrase position (raised high before low; falling high/low on the final syllable of a final IP; raised low on the final syllable of a non-final IP).
new_statements.domain_note: Howren's prosodic description is at the level of the intonational phrase and the syllable; tone is a syllable property. The Jaker abstract concerns the Wıìlıìdeh/Weledeh dialect (Dettah/N'dilo), not the Rae (Behchokǫ̀) dialect Howren describes.
new_statements.identity_note: Howren 1969 describes the conservative Fort Rae (Behchokǫ̀) dialect of Dogrib (dogr1252; no dialect glottocodes in Glottolog 5.3). The Jaker 2012/2026 work concerns the Wıìlıìdeh (Weledeh, Yellowknives Dene, Dettah/N'dilo) dialect, which Jaker treats under ISO dgr but as a distinct variety with reversed tones relative to Tetsǫ́t'ıné; Jaker's stress analysis should not be assumed to hold for Rae Dogrib without checking.

new_statements.quote: Data from two northern Dene languages, Tetsǫ́t’ıné (ISO: CHP) and Wıìlıìdeh (ISO: DGR) complicate this simple generalization. These two languages have nearly identical tonal phonologies, but with opposite tones. Early in the derivation, iambic stress attracts High tone in Tetsǫ́t’ıné, but Low tone in Wıìlıìdeh. However, later in the derivation, High tone attracts stress in both languages.
new_statements.citation: Jaker, Alessandro M. (2026). How Natural Is Tonal Phonology? What Happens to Stress-Tone Interactions When Tones Reverse? Linguistic Inquiry, doi:10.1162/ling.a.556 (CC-BY) — abstract only
new_statements.locator: Abstract, as carried in the Crossref record for 10.1162/ling.a.556 (same text in the Semantic Scholar record saved beside it); the MIT Press full text could not be opened by automated download
new_statements.reading: By the author of the 2012 Weledeh dissertation: Weledeh/Wıìlıìdeh Dogrib has iambic (right-headed) foot structure, and stress interacts with tone in two stages — stress attracts Low tone early and High tone attracts stress later. This is an abstract-level statement; it does not give the direction of footing or the position of primary word stress, so it supports a coding of 'iambic, quantity/tone-interacting' but not a specific edge. The full-text sources for the edge and the foot parse are Jaker 2012 (diss., 808 pp., ProQuest/Stanford) and Jaker 2017 (ANLA Working Papers 13 pp. 89-103, print only), both unobtained. The only full-text first-hand source read (Howren 1969, Rae dialect) is silent on stress.

These two languages have nearly identical tonal phonologies, but with opposite tones. Early in the derivation, iambic stress attracts High tone in Tetsǫ́t’ıné, but Low tone in Wıìlıìdeh. sources.locator: abstract (Crossref and Semantic Scholar records; full text blocked: MIT Press an automated-access block never clears by automated download even in headless Chrome; no archived copy at the Internet Archive; Unpaywall lists only the publisher copy)
sources.note: First-hand (author of the 2012 dissertation): Wıìlıìdeh/Weledeh Dogrib has iambic stress; at an early derivational level stress attracts Low tone (the mirror image of Tetsǫ́t’ıné, where it attracts High), and at a later level High tone attracts stress in both languages. The abstract does not say from which word edge feet are built or which syllable of the word carries primary stress; the body (unread) presumably does.
